title: Cloud Security Posture Management
summary: Cloud security posture management is the continuous, API-driven assessment of cloud configuration against an expected baseline. Tools connect with read-only credentials, enumerate resources across accounts and regions, evaluate each setting against policy, and re-evaluate as resources change, which is what separates posture management from a point-in-time review. Findings typically cover publicly reachable storage, permissive network rules, unencrypted volumes, disabled logging and dormant administrative identities. Posture management is distinct from workload protection, which watches running compute, and from entitlement analysis, which examines who can do what with which permissions. It appears in compliance reporting and in daily operations, where findings are routed to owners with a severity and a due date. The frequent mistake is treating the tool as the outcome. Teams generate a long list of findings, admire the dashboard, and close nothing, so the same misconfiguration returns with the next deployment because it was never fixed in the build template.

beginner.definition: Cloud security posture means the overall health of the settings in your cloud account. Cloud security posture management is a tool that reads those settings and warns you when one of them is risky. For example, it may tell you that a storage area is open to the whole internet. It checks many accounts at once and repeats the check all day.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most cloud breaches start with a setting that someone chose for speed and then forgot to change. A single open storage area can expose millions of customer records. Nobody can check thousands of settings by hand every day. A posture tool finds these mistakes early and shows which ones matter most. Without it, you learn about the problem from a journalist instead of your own dashboard.
howItWorks: The tool connects to your cloud account with read only permission and lists the resources you own.
It compares each resource setting against rules your team wrote or a published benchmark describes.
It marks each difference as a finding, with a severity level based on how exposed the resource is.
It then watches for changes, so a new public storage area raises an alert within minutes.
Good tools link each finding to an owner and to a fix. That fix may be a code change or a console setting.
You track the findings until they are closed, and record the few you accept as a known risk.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel inspector who walks the building every night with a checklist. The inspector does not cook or clean. Instead, the inspector looks for fire doors propped open, keys left in locks, and cameras that stopped recording. Each problem is written on a list with the room number and the person who should fix it. In the morning the manager works through that list. A cloud posture tool is the inspector, your cloud account is the hotel, and the checklist is your security policy.
takeaways: A posture tool only reports problems, so a person must own the fix and the deadline.
Prioritise findings that are reachable from the internet or that expose sensitive data, not the longest list.
Fix the settings in your build templates as well, or the same mistake returns with the next deployment.

objectives: Explain what cloud security posture management does and the problem it solves.
Describe how agentless posture tools collect configuration data from a cloud provider.
Distinguish posture management from workload protection and from entitlement analysis.
Explain how findings are prioritised and remediated in a real operations workflow.
Recognise the limits of configuration scanning, including gaps in runtime behaviour.
